title: Op Cost Analysis of Player-Facing Tool Selection Interfaces in Simulation Games
abstract: No standard unit exists for measuring the cost of player actions in game user interfaces. Design discussions rely on subjective preference, playtester sentiment, or A/B testing without a shared unit of measurement. This paper applies the op — the universal unit of information under action, defined in HOWL-INFO-14-2026 — to the specific domain of tool selection interfaces in simulation games. The op counts every discrete cognitive and physical action a player must perform to complete a task. Six domain-specific op categories are defined (look-at, read, scan, hover, move, click), each with fixed counting rules calibrated to game UI patterns. A library of compound actions provides pre-computed op costs for common UI interactions. Twelve benchmark tasks provide a standardized measurement surface for cross-game comparison. Measurements are taken across six commercial titles in two genres: colony simulation (Oxygen Not Included, Dwarf Fortress Steam Edition, RimWorld) and grand strategy (Europa Universalis IV, Crusader Kings III, Total War: Warhammer III). Results show that text-labeled hierarchical menus with keyboard acceleration produce the lowest combined new-player and expert interaction cost. Icon-only hierarchies produce the lowest expert cost but the highest new-player cost. Persistent icon grids produce the lowest within-category switching cost but the highest regression vulnerability. The framework makes these tradeoffs quantifiable, reproducible, and falsifiable.
